newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hebron imbroglio opens fault line in Israeli right.
newsitem.headline: Hebron imbroglio opens fault line in Israeli right.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu has yet to order a long-awaited Hebron pullout, but the issue has already caused an earthquake in Israeli politics, leaving religious rightists isolated and dismayed, analysts and politicians said.
A six-week marathon of exhausting talks has failed to seal an accord over the withdrawal from most of the West Bank town sacred to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of Abraham.

Yet by promising to honour the peace deal he reluctantly inherited with his election in May, Prime Minister Netanyahu stands to become the first leader of his rightist Likud to relinquish control over part of biblical Israel.
Analysts say that for Israel to make any progress beyond Hebron, Netanyahu will have to shake off his religious rightist allies -- or force them to let him move forward on peace.

Analyst Hanan Crystal said that 13 months after voting en masse to reject the previous Labour government's accord with the PLO on issues including the Hebron pullout, Likud and other rightist figures are poised to say yes to the troop withdrawal.

"They are willing to go along, to see (PLO leader) Yasser Arafat as a 'friend', and this constitutes an earthquake on the right - they have in effect moved to the centre, and left the National Religious Party (NRP) isolated with the extreme right."

The isolation and alarm felt by Israel's religious right -- once the much-heralded standard bearers of Likud ideology as expressed in Jewish settlements across the West Bank and Gaza -- has deepened with the first concrete signs of the pullout.
To the settlers' alarm, the Israeli public has watched with equanimity as some army units have left parts of the town.
Settlers last week took up positions beside Netanyahu's office and home, demonstrating against the very prime minister they toiled mightily to elect six months ago.

The settlers, who oppose any withdrawal as placing Hebron's Jews in danger, have blasted Netanyahu for not insisting on tougher security steps and greater leeway for settlers to expand their enclave beyond a few houses in the heart of the town.
Netanyahu publicly maintains the Hebron pact must be reworked to build in stronger safeguards for the 400 settlers and seminary students in the flashpoint town of more than 100,000 Palestinians.
But religious rightists say they have lost faith in Netanyahu, calling him no better than his dovish predecessor Shimon Peres.
"You promised, we believed, you betrayed," read a sign held by a protester outside Netanyahu's Jerusalem home.
Even the NRP, which holds nine seats in the 120-member parliament, is showing signs it may swallow a Hebron pullout in order to stay in the government, further isolating militant Jews.

NRP deputy cabinet minister Yigal Bibi, backpedaling on the party's hardline Hebron stance, suggested some religious rightists were resigned to the idea that a significant majority of Israelis backed a withdrawal.

Using the prime minister's nickname, he told Israel Television on Saturday: "Even our NRP is no longer talking extremism. It is speaking about minimal things, maybe 10 percent of what Bibi Netanyahu promised the voters."

Finance Minister Dan Meridor said in remarks broadcast on Saturday that Netanyahu's Likud and Peres's Labour should join forces in a "national unity" coalition to clinch elusive present and future agreements in the sluggish Israeli-PLO peace process.
"Very difficult questions remain open," Meridor told the television. "If we want to conduct these talks and reach good results, the best way is a national unity government."
Among unresolved core issues are the fate of Arab East Jerusalem, the settlements and Palestinian refugees. Talks on these are frozen pending a breakthrough on the Hebron impasse.
Even in opposition, Labour has promised to supply Netanyhau a parliamentary "safety net" to assure passage of peace moves should his hardline partners refuse to vote with him.

Tel Aviv Mayor Roni Milo -- whose support of the original interim accord nearly resulted in his expulsion from Likud -- said the debate over Hebron could spur hawks to "recognition of, and reconciliation with, reality...which could bring about a real change in Israel's political map."

Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak on Sunday turned aside the talk of a unity government "at this stage". But he quickly added: "In Israeli politics a cautious man says 'at this stage' because conditions can change."
